value: The Principle of Explosion (Latin: *ex falso quodlibet*) asserts that from a contradiction, any statement can be logically inferred, rendering a formal system trivial by making all propositions provable. First demonstrated in the 12th century by William of Soissons, this principle underscored the catastrophic implications of inconsistency, profoundly impacting the foundations of mathematics with the discovery of paradoxes like Russell's paradox, which spurred the development of consistent set theories such as Zermelo–Fraenkel. The article illustrates this concept with an example and explains its symbolic representation, further noting that alternative logical systems, known as paraconsistent logics, have been devised to accommodate contradictions without allowing a complete collapse of truth values, thereby maintaining meaningful distinctions within the system.
